steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Sociology is the systematic study of society, social institutions, and social relationships. It investigates how society shapes human behaviour, attitudes and life chances. C. Wright Mills called this the 'sociological imagination' - seeing the link between personal troubles and public issues.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Sociology vs common sense: common sense is based on everyday assumptions; sociology uses systematic research methods and evidence. Example: common sense says crime is rising; official statistics show it has fallen since the 1990s. Sociology tests claims against evidence.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Social structures are the organised patterns of relationships and institutions that shape society: family, education, religion, economy, government. They constrain individual behaviour but are also maintained by human action (structure vs agency debate).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Key perspectives overview: Functionalism (society as a system of interdependent parts), Marxism (society shaped by class conflict over economic resources), Feminism (society shaped by gender inequality), Interactionism (society created through everyday social interactions).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain the difference between sociology and common sense, using examples. | Describe what C. Wright Mills meant by the sociological imagination. | Evaluate whether individual behaviour is shaped more by social structures or personal agency.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Sociology = systematic, evidence-based study. Common sense = untested everyday assumptions. Personal troubles + public issues = sociological imagination (C. Wright Mills). Functionalism = consensus. Marxism = conflict. Feminism = gender inequality. Interactionism = meaning-making.
